newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia firm sees family values in video arcades.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia firm sees family values in video arcades.

text.p: Against a backdrop of official concerns about smoke-filled video arcades, one Malaysian firm is convinced family entertainment centres can be successful and is putting up the money to back its vision.
Super Merge Corp Sdn Bhd opened its first centre at a popular Kuala Lumpur shopping centre in mid-May, chief operating officer Noraini Abdullah told Reuters in an interview.
It plans to open some 20 more centres in three years with more than 100 million ringgit ($40 million), Noraini said.
"You used to have roomfuls of smoke and kids glued to these screens. Now people want something else," Noraini said. "We don't allow smoking and our centres are well-lighted."
The company, reputedly supported by Malaysian tycoon Halim Saad of conglomerate Renong Bhd, is expanding amid government threats not to renew licences of video arcade operators.
Selangor state chief minister Muhammad Muhammad Taib said recently he may allow video games rooms only at private clubs, saying they were causing social problems among teenagers.
Noraini, a former Renong executive, declined to confirm that Super Merge was backed by the politically well-connected Halim, saying only the company was linked to a "well-established businessmen".
She said Super Merge's first centre at Sungei Wang Plaza, may be a template for how video arcades of the future could allay government concerns.
The 10 million ringgit centre, called Sega Satellite, has the standard layout of wall-to-wall electronic video games, but includes extras not found in other arcades in the building.
These include virtual reality consoles and a Mazda MX-5 sports car hooked up for video racing.
One corner is dedicated to a 70-seat food and beverage (F&B) outlet, a first for video arcades in Malaysia.
"F&B is friendly to the family," she said. "The whole idea is to appeal to a broad section of people... so daddy can get his coffee while the kids play," she said.
Future arcades planned include those with virtual reality cafes, sports-themed centres and Internet stations, she said.
In an industry known in some places for its links with gangs, Noraini hopes a shake-out of the industry's image will dissuade authorities from closing it down.
"We want to demonstrate to the government that there is an alternative, that venues for video games can be healthy centres," Noraini said.

Super Merge's first centre is called Sega Satellite after Japan's top virtual reality firm, Sega Enterprises Ltd, which has a 20 percent stake in the company. Japanese conglomerate Mitsui & Co Ltd holds a 10 percent stake.
Pakatan Antara Sdn Bhd, widely believed by industry analysts to be controlled by Halim and his associates, has the majority equity of 70 percent.
Super Merge has a paid-up capital of 50 million ringgit, no small sum for a company incorporated just a year ago. It hopes to get a stock listing within four years.
Analysts said video arcades, banking on the growing affluence of the country after eight straight years of 8 percent annual economic growth, should continue to do well.
"It's a great business, which is riding on the economy. More wealth means more spare cash for fun," said an analyst at a local investment house.
Evidently seeing the potential from this entertainment venture, another major player recently announced plans to enter the fray.
Called Intencity, this chain of entertainment centres is the brainchild of Australia's Publishing & Broadcasting Ltd, Village Roadshow Ltd and Westfield Holdings Ltd.
Noraini said Intencity will be her biggest competitor. Most of the other video arcades in Malaysia are small centres operated by small-time businessmen.
($1 = 2.5 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom, 603-201-4813
